title: SRE standards: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, and runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's SRE standards for defining and operating Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, conducting capacity planning, running reliability initiatives, performing incident reviews, and authoring operational runbooks. It is intended for service owners, on-call engineers, product managers, and platform engineers responsible for production reliability.

Goals

- Provide a consistent SLO/SLO measurement framework across services.
- Define error budget policies and escalation paths.
- Give a repeatable capacity planning cadence and templates.
- Standardize incident review (postmortem) expectations and remediation tracking.
- Establish runbook quality standards and operational tooling requirements.

1) SLO & SLI standards

Definitions
- SLI (Service Level Indicator): the metric that captures user experience (e.g., successful inference responses per second, p50 latency of request to first token).
- SLO (Service Level Objective): the target value for an SLI over a specified rolling window (e.g., 99.9% availability over 30 days).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO target; the allowable failure budget for the window.

SLO template (required fields)
- service_name: short service identifier (e.g., runtime-inference-us-east-1)
- customer_facing: yes/no
- SLI_name and definition: clear measurement query (see examples below)
- target: e.g., 99.95% availability or p95 latency <= 150ms
- measurement_window: rolling 30d (default) or 7d for high-churn services
- alerting_thresholds: burn-rate and absolute thresholds (see section 3)
- owner: primary service owner (team and pager)
- related_dashboards: list of dashboard urls or ids

Required SLO table (every service must publish this in the service's Confluence page)

| service_name | SLI (query description) | target | window | owner | notes |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| runtime-inference-us-east-1 | successful_requests / total_requests (excludes client-side cancellations) | 99.95% | 30d | eng-serving-runtime | global-hosted API |
| model-loader | model-load-success / model-load-attempts | 99.9% | 30d | eng-serving-runtime | internal component |
| api-gateway | p95 request latency (ms) | <= 200ms | 30d | eng-platform | include cold-starts |

SLI measurement examples (PromQL / pseudo-queries)
- Availability SLI: sum(rate(http_request_total{status=~"2.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_request_total[5m]))
- Latency SLI: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))
- Successful inference: sum(rate(inference_response{result!~"error|timeout"}[5m])) / sum(rate(inference_requests_total[5m]))

2) Error budget policy and burn-rate controls

Error budget allocation and ownership
- Each service is assigned a rolling error budget equal to (1 - SLO) over the measurement window. The service owner is accountable for preventing budget exhaustion.
- Error budget can be used for planned changes (rollouts, experiments) provided a rollout risk assessment is recorded.

Burn-rate monitoring and automated actions
- Burn-rate is monitored over three windows: 5m, 1h, and 24h.
- Alerting thresholds (recommended default):
  - Warning: burn-rate > 2 for 1h (notify owner)
  - Action: burn-rate > 4 for 15m (page on-call)
  - Critical: burn-rate > 6 for 5m (trigger incident response and suspend risky rollouts)

Error budget playbook (1-3)
1. At Warning threshold: owner investigates recent deploys, traffic changes, and recent alerts; open an "error-budget-investigation" ticket and add to next weekly reliability sync.
2. At Action threshold: page on-call; roll back recent canary if correlation found; enable additional capacity (scale up) if capacity constraint detected.
3. At Critical threshold: declare incident, follow incident runbook, pause all non-emergency releases, and notify stakeholders (product and support).

3) Capacity planning standards

Cadence and inputs
- Major capacity planning cadence: quarterly (QBR) plus monthly operational forecasts.
- Required inputs for every capacity plan: historical qps and p95/p99 latency by route, burst characteristics (99.99th percentile), planned product launches, model catalog changes (larger model memory/latency), and capacity SLAs (Dedicated customers).

Headroom and safety margins
- Target steady-state headroom: 30% for hosted public API services, 40% for Dedicated pools with SLA commitments.
- Burst provisioning: ensure 99.9% of observed bursts can be absorbed via autoscaling/burst pools without SLO impact.

Capacity plan template (deliverable) - include as a Markdown/Confluence table
- current_peak_qps, projected_peak_qps_next_90d, headroom_required, delta_gpus_needed, expected_cost_delta, owner, mitigation_plan

Sizing guidance and examples
- Example: service handles 10k inference requests/s peak; p95 latency 120ms on A100-80GB with batching profile X. To meet 30% headroom for anticipated 50% growth, add N GPUs (detailed calculation included in spreadsheet template linked on page).

4) Reliability initiatives and technical debt remediation

Classification and prioritization
- Reliability initiatives should be classified as Critical, High, Medium, or Low based on customer impact, recurrence, and cost to fix.
- Prioritization criteria: frequency of incidents, customer impact (SLA violations), operational toil, and cross-team dependency.

Typical initiatives
- Improve observability: add end-to-end tracing for request lifecycle through routing, cache, and runtime.
- Reduce cold-starts: optimize model loader pre-warming and keep-alive policies.
- Failover hardening: implement model-variant fallbacks and regional routing.
- Automated mitigations: circuit breakers, adaptive batching, and graceful degradation flows.

Success metrics and experiments
- Each initiative must have a measurable success metric (e.g., reduce incident MTTD by 30%, reduce p99 latency by 20%, reduce error budget burn by 50%). Use A/B rollouts with guarded canaries.

5) Incident review (postmortem) standards

Postmortem requirements (every Sev1/Sev2 incident)
- Title, incident lead, incident start/end timestamps, summary, impact (customer-visible effects, internal effects), root cause analysis, timeline of key events, corrective actions (immediate and long-term), owners, and verification criteria.
- Postmortems are expected within 5 business days and include a documented follow-up plan with dates and owners.

Root cause guidance
- Use the "5 whys" and include both technical and organizational contributing factors (on-call tooling gaps, change review failures, release process gaps).
- Avoid blame language; focus on system and process fixes.

Blameless review checklist (for reviewers)
- Did the postmortem include data and timelines?
- Are corrective actions specific, measurable, and assigned?
- Is there an owner and expected completion date for each action?
- Were related services notified and updated?

6) Runbook & operational tooling standards

Runbook quality criteria (required)
- One-line purpose statement.
- Preconditions: what must be true before runbook steps are executed (e.g., telemetry available, access rights).
- Quick triage checklist (5 bullet steps to determine class of incident).
- Step-by-step mitigation actions with exact CLI/console commands, dashboard links, and expected outcomes.
- Escalation contacts and contact-info (pager duty, slack channel, manager).
- Post-incident verification steps and rollback instructions.
- Last verified date and runbook owner.

Operational tooling minimums
- Dashboards: SLO dashboard (30d rolling), Error budget burn dashboard, Capacity and utilization charts, On-call run-rate (alerts/hour) chart.
- Alerting: PagerDuty (or equivalent) for Action/Critical thresholds; email/slack for Warning. Alerts must include runbook link and a short remediation hint.
- Tracing & logs: end-to-end traces with request_id propagation; structured logs with correlation ids; centralized indexing (e.g., Elastic/Logs).
- Chaos & game days: quarterly game-days covering cold-starts, region failover, and autoscaler behavior.

7) Ownership, reviews, and governance

- Every service must publish SLOs and runbooks in its Confluence page and list an SLO owner. The SRE org performs a quarterly SLO review with product and platform stakeholders.
- The reliability steering group (representatives from eng-sre, eng-serving-runtime, product, and solutions engineering) meets monthly to review high-impact postmortems, approve major reliability initiatives, and track progress.

Appendix: Quick reference of common alerts and actions

- High inference 5xx rate -> check model health, recent deployments, and model-serving queue length; scale inference pool; open incident if > 0.5% of traffic sustained for 10m.
- Rising p99 latency -> check GPU saturation, kernel errors, batching backlog; increase batch size if acceptable; spin up additional nodes.
- Error budget burn during deploy -> abort rollout and roll back to previous stable model variant.
